stem: The relation R on the set of integers Z defined by R = {(a, b) : a - b is divisible by 3} is an equivalence relation. How many equivalence classes does R partition Z into?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Thinking all integers are related to each other because 'divisibility by 3 connects everything', missing that the classes are the residues 0, 1, 2 mod 3.
Thinking in terms of even and odd parity (divisibility by 2) and incorrectly applying that pattern to divisibility by 3, giving two classes instead of three.

Two integers a and b are in the same class exactly when a - b is divisible by 3, meaning they have the same remainder when divided by 3. The possible remainders are 0, 1, and 2, giving exactly 3 equivalence classes: multiples of 3, integers leaving remainder 1, and integers leaving remainder 2.
Confusing the number of elements in Z with the number of equivalence classes; each integer forms its own 'class' thinking only in terms of the set size rather than the partition structure.

explanation: Divisibility by 3 partitions Z into exactly 3 residue classes corresponding to remainders 0, 1, and 2.

explanation_sections.punchline: Congruence modulo n always creates exactly n equivalence classes: the n residue classes mod n.
explanation_sections.approach: State the property then contrast the confusable one. An equivalence relation partitions its set into equivalence classes where each element belongs to exactly one class. For 'a - b divisible by 3': a ~ b iff a mod 3 = b mod 3. There are exactly 3 possible remainders (0, 1, 2) when dividing by 3, so exactly 3 classes. The trap is confusing the number of classes with the size of the set Z (infinite) or with divisibility by 2 (which gives 2 classes).
explanation_sections.lesson: Congruence modulo n on Z always produces exactly n equivalence classes, one for each residue 0, 1, ..., n-1.
explanation_sections.timing: About 75 seconds. Identify this as congruence mod 3, count the distinct remainders. The trap is sliding to mod 2 thinking.
